text: Please stay tuned for important disclosure information at the conclusion of this episode.
Hi, and welcome to the Long View. I'm Amy Arnott, portfolio strategist for Morningstar.
And I'm Christine Benz, director of personal finance and retirement planning for Morningstar.
Our guest on the podcast today is Joseph Moore, a historian and author of the best-selling book
How to Get Rich in American History, 300 years of financial advice that worked and didn't,
where he chronicles all of the various things Americans have tried to do to get ahead over three centuries.
He's also an investor who went from being an academic to funding a tech startup, buying land on the moon,
founding a cryptocurrency, and owning dozens of investment properties.
So, Christine, this was a really fun conversation where we covered a lot of ground
about the history of financial advice in the U.S. as well as Joseph's own adventures in investing and money-making ventures.
And one of the really interesting things he said, I thought, was that who you marry is actually a really strong indicator of financial success.
I really like that part of the conversation too, Amy, as well as his discussion of the secret role of women in household financial decision-making.
I also thought Joseph's conversation of what he calls the despair industrial complex was incredibly thought-provoking.
Yeah, those were all highlights for me too.
All right, so let's roll the tape.
Joseph, welcome to the long view.
I am so excited to be here. Thank you for having me.
Well, we're excited to have you.
You started out as a college professor, and I wanted to ask, how did you first get involved in real estate investing and writing about financial history,
and what gave you the idea to write this book?
Dodging a bullet is the answer to that question.
So, it's 2006, I think.
My wife and I were graduate students, and back then the lesson of history supposedly was clear.
Everybody told you the lesson of history was renting, was throwing your money away.
And instead of thinking about that like a historian, because I was literally getting a PhD in history as a graduate student,
I nodded my head like everybody else did, and we got, we're both graduate students, and we got a no-income verification loan to buy a townhouse,
which sounds as ridiculous today as it was then, but nobody thought it was ridiculous then.
Fast forward to 2008, our church offers a personal finance class for families.
We went, they made us fill a budget, we go home.
My wife goes to sleep, I did not sleep a wink.
I literally paced the house all night, because I was thinking, who gave us a mortgage?
We have no business owning anything. We're graduate students.
And so, we put our house on the market, it's sold on a Saturday, and the reason I remember the Saturday is because the following Saturday,
our neighbor put her house on the market, and it never sold.
So, it was the 2008 Titanic had sunk, and we were the last two people off of it.
And I just kind of woke up intellectually and thought, why did I not think like a historian?
So, I had no business training whatsoever.
But I wanted to come at this topic as a historian would to ask, what were people told to do?
Did it work? And if so, what can we learn from that?
And so, that began kind of an over a decade long journey of trying to find absolutely every scrap of financial advice I could discover in American history.
And as it turns out, what everyone thought always worked was always changing.
And so, in every generation, people finally feel like, well, we finally figured out finance and what to do to actually get ahead.
And that it changes. And, you know, generation by generation, people have to adapt.
And that's one of the things that you kind of take away from studying the past is we think the past is this stable thing.
And we are what moves through time.
But the mean is moving behind you.
And we can learn a lot by seeing how much change other generations had to endure.
And, you know, I got lucky and endured that change on the right side of the 08 financial crisis.
So we want to delve into some of the lessons that we can all learn from history.
But we wanted to stick with your background a little bit.
You decided to use what you know about history to make a million dollars.
And you actually succeeded at that.
Did you always have a more practical bent than the typical academic?
And I'm curious what people in your circle, your academic circle, thought about your money making efforts?
Oh, no, they thought I was crazy, bluntly.
So look, I have a lot of dear academic friends who kind of cross all ideological spectrums.
But there is a tendency in academia, especially in the humanities where I reside,
to think and talk very grandly about the working class.
Very few of the people who make such statements are actually from themselves, the working class.
And I was raised in rural South Carolina.
You know, I come from where the money was not found.
Nobody in my family had money.
I didn't know anybody.
I didn't know a single person in my entire life until I probably was in my 30s who went to Ivy League school.
So like, there was just, this was a world apart from most academic backgrounds.
I have a fun game I play with myself when I'm in academic conferences.
We're sitting around shooting the breeze, drinking a beer or something.
And I'll ask people, where'd you go to high school?
Because they're not ready for that question.
They are thinking, where'd you go to grad school?
Where'd you do your undergrad?
And so they'll just tell you, and I'll go look it up.
And almost inevitably, it's like the most elite public education school or a preparatory academy somewhere.
And I'm like, don't you write books about the working class?
But I can't, you know, my father used to climb underneath mobile homes and inspect electrical wire.
Like that was his job.
He made $14,000 a year for a long time.
And so I was just raised around the trades.
I was raised around guys who, you know, did working class jobs and we had a working class life.
And it didn't occur to me to not have those values.
And I remember when I got into academia, I was shocked because it was the first time I met people who would tell me,
without thinking about it, that something was beneath them.
Like, I wouldn't do that. That's beneath me.
And I was like, something's, it had never occurred to me that something was beneath me to do.
And so, yes, I do have a more practical bent, I think, than the average, especially humanities academic.
And that led me to see things differently.
And I think one of the, one of the things that's been a joy of his book tour is that in the world of finance,
the reason my book is so different is that it, I didn't take any of the financial assumptions for granted that everyone just assumes are there.
I asked different questions.
And from the academic perspective, it never occurred to me that those questions weren't worth asking.
And hopefully that's led to a unique, a unique book. Certainly.
It's been a crazy ride for me.
Yeah, it definitely is unique and also very funny. So I really enjoyed reading it.
Thank you. That was intentional. I really wanted it to be a fun read.
I mean, I told somebody, I wanted to write a history of everyday people's finances that everyday people would enjoy reading.
And so that's been one of the most rewarding things is hearing people say they enjoyed it, you know, that it's fun to read.
Because I remember when it was fun to read, so we need more books that are fun to read.
Yeah, especially about finance.
So one of the very first ideas you introduce in the book is the phrase go ahead.
And you write that this was sort of like a 19th century Internet meme that meant moving to a better place than you began.
Can you expand a little bit on what that phrase means and what makes this idea of going ahead uniquely American?
Yeah, so the subtitle of the book is 300 years of financial advice that worked and didn't.
And very few people have picked up on that. But the reason I did 300 years was that predates the American Revolution.
And to some extent, what is the first uniquely American financial advice?
And that advice is basically this. If you look around you in the poverty stricken town in which you live,
England, Scotland, later Italy, parts of China, Japan.
If you will get on this rickety boat for roughly two months,
then you can actually have a chance to get on the property ladder and move up with your life and go ahead from where you are to a better place.
And your children will have a chance to do the same.
Now, that sounds inspiring, you know, on our side of the boat, but if you're on the other side of the boat, that's a risk reward proposition.
It's not entirely clear it will work out. And to be clear, there are some people for whom it does not work out.
Some of those boats didn't land in places that worked out.

But the idea that you could take a risk to move your family from a place that you would never get ahead to one where your family could actually see a better life at the end of yours was a uniquely American proposition at the time.
You had to actually get on the boat and do it.
And so that idea pervades the 19th century especially.
Now, people would talk about this in newspapers, in books, in bars.
Men, women, like people said, it's a go ahead culture.
They commented on this over and we're a go ahead, not get ahead.
We talk about getting ahead like it happens to you.
But their assumption was that go ahead was something you had to get up and go do.
And this crossed decades and the whole of the 1800s.
It was a white idea, a black idea.
I mean, Frederick Douglass, the famous abolitionist.
We remember him mostly for his speech, What to the Slave is the Fourth of July, which is an incredible speech.
We teach it in schools. I've taught it. We should continue to teach it.
But in his lifetime, that was even close to his most famous speech.
Far and away, his most famous speech was called Self Made Men.
And in that speech, now the gendered term there is just the term of the time he means men and women.
But the idea of that speech, the crescendo line is maybe I cannot be president.
He says as a black man in the 1870s, but I can be prosperous.
And you have to think about like everywhere he went, white audiences and black audiences were calling out for that speech.
And after he says I can be prosperous, he says our motto is go ahead.
And that idea was pervasive and one that we've largely lost.
We think getting ahead happens to you.
They thought that you happened to it.
So a central idea of the book is that getting ahead or maybe going ahead is easier than ever.
But we constantly see headlines about student debt, housing affordability, economic decline.
And I would say that statistics I've seen on economic mobility in the U.S. are pretty persuasive that it's not really what it once was.
But maybe you can talk about that issue, why the media narrative is so negative and often it odds with historical evidence.
So there's kind of two ways we could take that conversation.
One is the rhetorical conversation and one is the statistics.
So let's do the rhetorical first.
Rhetorically, I can find people telling you the American dream is dead probably 300 years before I can find the actual phrase American dream, which comes up in the 1930s.
So in the 1670s, this is 100 years before Hamilton is going to wrap on Broadway.
In the 1670s, the colonists of Virginia burned their own capital to the ground in anger because no one could get ahead anymore.
That was from the very beginning.
There's been rhetoric around no one's getting ahead.
You arrive too late.
There's big speeches in the 1800s saying this.
One of my prized possessions is a 1984 bestselling book sold nearly 100,000 copies that said that the baby boomers would never be able to afford to retire.
And so the rhetoric is very old.
I call this big whoa, a kind of despair industrial complex because there's no clicks for a journalist.
There's no votes for a politician.
Heck, there's no tenure for an academic like me if I just get up and tell everybody that the world is getting better.
But I can have all of those things if I tell you it's getting worse.
So there's kind of the people who are giving that message out are actually being empowered by that message to implement their solutions or to monetize their traffic or whatever it is.
But you actually end up getting penalized for listening because if you believe no one gets ahead, then you will not take the actions necessary to get ahead.
So there's the rhetorical part of it.
Let's move to the statistical part of it.
There's two buckets of those mobility statistics.
One of them is wrong and the other one I will take and use and flip on its head and show that it actually shows it's a lot better than you think it does.
The first set of statistics that came out about mobility showed that the 1800s had this wildly rapid upward mobility in America and it's declined ever since.
The problem with those statistics is they were almost all taken from Iowa.
The thing about Iowa is that it's not really representative of the whole of the United States.
It just happened to have a particularly good data set.

And so a lot of the early mobility stats that celebrated how fast people could get ahead in the 1800s and early 20th century and then had the decline of it basically had forgotten about a lot of poor people,
especially minorities who are just aren't in the data.
And so when you combine the actual different demographic data sets, you find that mobility has gotten faster, not slower.
Well, we forget how impoverished early Americans really were.
Then you look at something like the Ross Chetty famous paper in science that talks about, you know, basically mobility of Americans peaked for the generation born right after World War Two,
that they got ahead of their parents faster than any generation and then it slows down after 1980.
Okay, first of all, what they're really measuring is moving from the bottom to the middle class and for the chance to go from the bottom to the middle, that is probably true.
However, their parents were living through the Great Depression.
So this is a kind of skewed data set.
This idea that like, well, my parents lived through the worst economic collapse in history and I'm doing pretty well.
Is it necessary?
It's, you know, the reality is the quality of life that we're living today absolutely dwarfs the quality of life of the early baby boomers.
So when I look at that stat, I say, okay, what do we see? This is the Chetty data that I'm using.
If you look at people born in the bottom fifth, six and 10 will get out in their own lifetime.
That is not perfect mobility, which would be eight and 10, but it's not that far off.
Four and 10 make it to the middle class.
One in 10 go all the way from the bottom all the way to the top.
That is compared to the rest of human history, mind blowing upward mobility.
The flip side of that is downward mobility.
Of children born in the top fifth, six and 10 will fall out in their own lifetime, which is the exact same as Denmark.
So we have a rhetoric around mobility that is kind of skewed to the idea of one generation's experience.
But when you pan the camera back out, you look over 300 years of history, Americans are getting ahead faster than our ancestors could have ever dreamed we could have.
You also note that your father hated rich people and it seems like that's sort of a growing attitude in the country now.
We see lots of resentment toward the wealthy and interest in taxing billionaires, things like that.
Why has hostility toward wealth remained such a persistent part of American culture?
So I think there's, I mean, that's a great question, by the way.
I don't want to pretend that I'm going to unlock that mystery in a couple of minutes, but I'd probably take it in two kind of general ideas.
One is the kind of upward mobility motif that is the American dream or go ahead, as I used to say.
There was an empowerment of people at the bottom that was very unusual compared to any other place in the world at the time.
And that gave people a voice to decry anything.
I mean, the free press may be honestly part of the answer.
Just the idea that you lived in a nation where such opinions could be freely expressed without fear of retribution from said elites and rich people was somewhat unique.
And so the ability to print those ideas and those complaints, there may have been those complaints for all of history, but you can't read them very often.
I mean, you get the levelers in England and these, but that's not common.
But I think the other thing, the reason that we seem to think it's getting more loud today.
I think we probably misjudge how local life used to be and how national media landscape has become in the sense that most people's experience with the rich was local.
It was the local elites that they knew.
They may know the Rockefellers exist, but they've never met one.
They've never walked past their Park Avenue homes and had to like gawk at them and wonder why they have to live in a tiny apartment.
Some New Yorkers might, but most people in the country are living a very local life.
And now we have a very nationalized media.
And so if you go over to the previous time that we have an explosion of kind of critiques of wealth from a kind of socialist perspective, the way we're seeing now.
The last time was around the presidency of Eugene Debs and kind of started with the populist angst about the railroads.
Well, what was happening with railroads and radio is an era in which we're nationalizing our economy and our media.
So anytime local people are suddenly confronted with narratives about national elites that they'll I've never met Elon Musk and probably never will probably won't see him with my own eyes.
But I'm very aware of him in a way I would not be if my media consumption and my life was entirely local.
And most people's lives generally were.
One of the books main ideas is you live most of your life in slow time and that's a quote you get rich and fast time.
Maybe you could talk a bit more about what that means.
So most of us don't think a lot about financial history.
It's not it's not top of mind for most of us.
We wake up in the morning.
If we ever think about financial history at all, almost certainly it's what I call fast time history.
That's when everything is changing everywhere all at once to quote the movie and a handful of smart people saw it coming.
Everybody else got wiped out and you just don't want to be the dumb people.
It's always 1929.
It's always 2008.
And the problem with those histories is not that they're not good and fun.
They are.
But they're not written to teach you what to do with your money.
They are written to entertain you and they're very good at that.
Like you are supposed to flip the page or look at the movie screen and scream, you know, he's behind you.
The subprime mortgage lender is behind you run away from the mortgage.
That's what you're supposed to do with those histories and they're very good at that.
But they're not there to teach you what to actually do with your money because most of financial history is not fast time.
Most change is slow and imperceptible.
And by the way, that doesn't mean it's quiet.
It could be very loud in fast time.
One of my favorite things to do when I'm giving public talks, I go around like I give talks and, you know, different organizations or whatever.
And I will put on the screen two quotes from the New York Times.
And one essentially says a depression is right around the corner.
And one says a booming economy is right around the corner.
And I tell people these are less than three months apart.
Headlines of the New York Times.
Now, guess the year.
And people will, you know, hands go up 1939, 19, you know, 2007, 2008, 1929, 1930.
I tell them it's 1948.
And then I ask if anyone can remember anything that happened in 1948.
And usually most people cannot because it was a very boring historical year, especially for markets.
And yet people were screaming in the headlines that boom or bust was right around the corner.
So slow time can be very loud.
But most of your life is lived with people being loud and volatility kind of staying within a normal range.
And that's where most of your financial life will be lived.
That's where most of your financial decisions will be made.
And it's the decisions you make in slow time that can be stress tested in fast time.
And people usually leap ahead in fast time.
Any business owner knows this.
They'll have a phrase something like you work and you work and you work and nothing happens and then out of nowhere everything breaks.
And that's most financial life.
You also argue that people should take more risks.
What kind of risks are actually worth taking?
Yeah. So let's first of all, let's define risk because some people can hear that and think, you know, put out a HELOC on the house and put it all on Bitcoin, which is gambling.
And the difference between gambling and risk could be summarized simply as do you have some measurable impact on the outcome?
You know, I can't affect the price of Bitcoin.
Nothing I'm going to do will shake it.

But I can have some measurable impact on a whole lot of other risks that I take, whether it's an investment property that I'm going to turn around, whether it's an investment in a small business that I'm going to, you know, run better.
Whether it's a rearrangement of my investment portfolio so that I'm putting away more money than I otherwise would.
But like if I have some control over what's happening, then at least it's a risk, not a gamble.
And I think most risks, if you go back through history, the idea that most of your risks worth taking were all in the market would have not made any sense to anyone.
Even business leaders would not have understood that.
Most of your risks were going to be in your business or your career.

One of the things I think people can misread in much of the literature, including in my book, you've got to be careful, is I'm not saying quit your job and go start a small business and risk it all there.
There's ways to risk in business and there's ways to risk inside of another business, like taking a salary from somebody else's business.
But what I think has happened in the course of the last four to five decades is because the baby boomers have had such a wild, successful run of having their retirement savings make them rich,
we have assumed that the way you get rich is by slowly steadily putting money away in low-risk assets.
That usually did not work in history.
So the risks we're taking, the first one is in your career.
You know, when young people, if I'll talk to young people and they'll say, you know, should I be putting $100, $200 a month away in the stock market?
Sure, sounds like a great idea.
But just a quick question, is there a credential that you could go get that would help you in the next five years double your salary?
Put your money on that.
I mean, I met a guy researching the book who's never been to college, makes a fabulous salary because he's gotten every credential in the industry for airline mechanics.
And you literally can't take the plane apart and put it back together, which you have to do every so many miles unless he signs off on it.
He's doing great because he invested in his career.
There's a big difference in the income of an entry-level nurse and a nurse anesthetist.
And so, first and foremost, invest in your career, invest in getting better and better so that your income can grow by an exponent.
But then there's small business.
I mean, that really is one of the ways most deco-millionaires and above got to that point was by owning, investing in a small business.
And we have more such deco-millionaires and above than we've ever had in American history, even adjusted for inflation, by the way.
And most of those people are doing very un-sexy jobs in industries you've never thought of.
Like, the Wall Street Journal ran a thing on these men and women who were doing this, one of whom has a carpet removal company specializing in over-the-summer carpet removal.
Because schools, when they need new carpet, they've got like 60 days max to pull that off.
And you've got a whole school.
And he's just specialized in removing carpet for schools.
And he's, you know, worth 10 million.
And I've interviewed so many people like this in research in the book who are doing things you would have never thought to do.
So take the risk in your own career, in small business.
I think those are risks we're taking.
So if most wealth is created in occasional bursts rather than a steady march upward, how should investors position themselves for those fast-time moments?
So that's a great question, too.
I'm working on an essay on this from my sub-stack right now.
I have it wrestled down, but I want to make it interesting and fun to read.
So that's the part.
How do you make social sciences equations fun to read?
It's not always an easy circle to square.
But it basically boils down to this.
The equation is going to look something like this.
You're going to have volatility, which you can't predict.
You're going to have concentration of assets, which you control.
You decide how concentrated your risk profile is.
And then the other things you can control outside of that is how much liquidity do you have against how urgent are your debt deadlines?
Not the amount of debt you have, but the payment schedule for that debt.
And people who are in different industries know that debt works very differently in different industries.
If you have a lot of debt, but it's all in 3.5% mortgages on rental properties, your debt deadlines are pretty easy to manage.
If you've got a balloon note coming due in 18 months, that is much harder to manage.
So if fast time hits when you have a low liquidity and a looming debt deadline, you can get wiped out quickly.
And so needing to manage the liquidity versus the deadlines for your debt is one part of that.
But the other part is the concentration.
Fast time rewards and punishes concentration.
So when fast time comes, when everything shifts, the people who are concentrated in the areas that it's in are the ones who outperform everyone else.
Because of the concentration when everything shifted.
And of course, the same thing to the downside.
And so you have to think very strategically about where do I want to be concentrated when change comes.
And when that change comes, especially if it comes in the way I wasn't expecting, can I survive it by looking at the relationship to my liquidity and the debt deadlines that I have to carry?
And now that's, again, you can see why it's a struggle to make that essay fun to read.
But you just have to understand that financial time and regular time don't work on the same speed.
So imagine I put on your wrist a regular, perfectly timed wristwatch.
And then I take another clock and I take it to the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.
The one on your wrist is going to tick with everyone else's time.
But the one on the stock exchange is going to tick for every normal second of financial activity.
On the average month, the clock on your wrist and the clock on the stock exchange are going to roughly, you know, they're going to align pretty well.
Because there's an average month with an average amount of up and down.
And so they're going to stay aligned.
But every now and again, that clock on the stock exchange speeds up incredibly or goes backwards.
And so financial time can operate at a different speed than the time of the life you're living.
And so you want to be concentrated in the right places when that happens.
And you want to be able to survive it if you're concentrated in the wrong places.
We also wanted to ask you a couple of questions about the history of financial advice, which you also cover in the book.
And you argue that financial advice as a profession emerged almost accidentally.
There was no job title of financial advisor before 1969.
Can you talk about how the profession of financial advice first got started?
Yeah, so let's go before the dawn of modern financial industry.
Where was most financial advice found?
And this surprised me because the trail went cold for me as a historian.
I'm basically a detective.
I'm reading Dead People's Mail trying to figure out what happened.
And the trail went cold right around 1910, 1912, where I ended up finding most financial advice before then was in housewife manuals.
Because the average housewife has to manage the whole family's income and out go.
Women's magazines are replete with financial advertisements for mortgage companies or investment opportunities.
So like women were really active in forming financial ideas and executing them.
And that's a part of history that's been completely lost.
Then something happens in 1912.
All financial advice before 1912 was kind of easy to understand.
Everyone knew what to do.
And that basically boiled down to, you know, if you were going to have paper investments,
you wanted to invest in bonds or dividend yielding stocks at about 5% because there was 0% inflation.
And then in 1912, when there's 0% inflation, everything changes.
Inflation goes from zero.
So 1912, a gallon of milk costs 24 cents a gallon.
If I go back in time to 1812, think about 1812 to 1912.
In 1812, Napoleon rules France and men wear hoes.
Like that's a different world than 1912.
And in 1912, inflation goes from 0% to the next year it goes 8, which is double where we are right now.
8, 18, 17, 17, 15 in five years.
Prices doubled.
There was not a mother, a grandmother or a great grandmother who knew what to do.
And everything that used to work stopped working.
And all the things that you used to be told not to do, like invest in stocks, started to work.
And so there's this explosion of financial literature in the 1910s and 20s about how to understand this new world and what to do.
But there's really not anybody to turn to who has mastered this and kind of codified it into a job description where they help you.
You can go to your banker and they can help you execute some things.
You can go to a broker, but most people don't have brokers and most people don't buy stocks.
That starts to shift in the 1960s.
Most people's financial purchases were one of two things.
If it was a market or put aside real estate, which was actually what most people spent their money on or invested their money with.
But let's go to the paper investments.
It was mutual funds and insurance.
That's what most people did.

And in the late 1960s, there were all kinds of scandals about just how egregious some of the sales techniques were for basically selling insurance products that were mostly good for the insurance company and selling mutual funds with huge fees.
I mean, fees that would make mutual fund advisors today feel embarrassed if they got.
And while that was great for the industry, it was bad for the average consumer and a group of mutual fund salesmen and insurance salesmen agree to have a meeting at the Chicago O'Hare Airport.
And I can't remember exactly how many.
It's not many.
It's maybe a dozen or so people fly in.
These are like the top selling mutual fund and insurance salesmen in the country.
And they all feel like this industry is kind of getting rotten and they don't want to be associated with that.
So they fly in, they have a meeting and they decide we're going to find a new entity, a nonprofit that's going to be financial advising.
So they fly in as insurance salesmen and mutual fund salesmen.
And they never leave O'Hare, by the way.
And then they fly out and they're financial advisors.
They change their title in that meeting.
And going forward, that idea spreads that you could have certified financial planners or financial advisors, different groups spring up to do it.
But that's a new thing in the 60s.
And in a way, I argue it's actually a really good thing.
Because prior to that, you couldn't really find anybody in your local community who could help you understand all of these different financial investments all at the same time.
So it's a new profession because it's an entirely new investing world.
You write in the book that Dave Ramsey has changed more people's personal finances than maybe anyone in history.
So why do academics and financial experts tend to look down on figures like Ramsey?
Well, I've always loved Morningstar.
So something tells me that the Morningstar audience is not going to like that.
You've got some very sophisticated financial listeners out there.
So let me make my case for why gurus get a bad rap, especially amongst professionals.
Finance professors have incredible equations that work very well on spreadsheets.
What gurus have is the awareness that Superbowl adds work.
Birthday sex leads to baby number three.
And I have yet to see a finance equation that models accurately a midlife crisis or a child with special needs.
When you live in the real world and it's dynamic and changing,
you need some rules of thumb.
And what you find when you look at studies of what people who read personal finance gurus actually remember,
it's not what's in the book.
It's what do you remember from the book?
And if I go to the average person who read a finance guru,
let's just pick one off the shelf that's particularly egregious, Rich Dad Poor Dad,
which I think we can all agree is an eye roll level book.
But the average person only remembers that they should buy assets
and that assets are defined very simply as things that make you money instead of cost you money.
